1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. IOPS: input/output operations per second; DAX: DynamoDB Accelerator; RDS: Relational Database Service; EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud; SSD: solid state drive; AZ: Availability Zone; OSS: open source software; SPARQL: SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language; DMS: Database Migration Service; SCT: Schema Conversion Tool

  • Choose a database type and engine from the access pattern
  • Plan capacity: instance classes, Provisioned IOPS, capacity units and serverless scaling
  • Configure read replicas, endpoints and connection handling
  • Integrate caching with ElastiCache, DAX and MemoryDB
  • Pick a path for homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations

2Database types, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, caching and purpose-built databases

Running case

Lantern and Loom Chooses Databases

  • Orders need transactions and SQL
  • Browsing the catalog is read-heavy
  • Shopping carts need millisecond lookups at any scale
  • Recommendations follow relationships between products
  • A self-managed MySQL server on EC2 must move to a managed service
  • Your job: match each need to a database

Database Types and Access Patterns

Type Service Best for
Relational RDS, Aurora Transactions, joins, SQL
Key-value and document DynamoDB Single-digit millisecond lookups at any scale
In-memory ElastiCache, MemoryDB Microsecond reads, caching, sessions
Document DocumentDB MongoDB-compatible JSON
Graph Neptune Highly connected data
Wide-column Keyspaces Cassandra workloads
  • Read-intensive: replicas and caches. Write-intensive: bigger instances, Provisioned IOPS, well-spread keys
Exam tip

Name the access pattern first: joins, lookups, relationships, documents or speed.

Amazon RDS Engines and Capacity [Verify live]

  • Managed engines: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2, plus Aurora
  • AWS runs backups, patching, failure detection and recovery; you tune queries
  • Instance classes: db.m general purpose, db.r, x, z memory optimized, db.c compute, db.t burstable
  • Storage: General Purpose SSD, or Provisioned IOPS for I/O-intensive production with consistent low latency
  • Multi-AZ for availability, read replicas for reads
  • As of 5 November 2026: Magnetic storage is deprecated; check the page
Exam tip

RDS is the default for relational; choose the engine your application and tools need.

Amazon Aurora

  • MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible; AWS cites up to 6 times the throughput of stock engines on similar hardware
  • The cluster volume grows automatically, up to 256 TiB, with data in three AZs
  • Up to 15 Aurora Replicas share that same storage, so lag is small, and one can take over after a failure
  • A reader endpoint spreads reads
  • Move from RDS MySQL or PostgreSQL by snapshot or replication

Exam tip

Relational, MySQL or PostgreSQL compatible, fast failover and many replicas: Aurora.

Aurora Serverless [Verify live]

  • An on-demand, autoscaling configuration of Aurora; capacity is measured in Aurora capacity units (ACUs)
  • It scales in steps as small as half an ACU, usually without pausing transactions
  • You set a minimum and maximum, and it can scale to zero with auto pause
  • Best for variable or unpredictable load, new apps, multi-tenant fleets and dev and test
  • Readers can scale on their own; a cluster can mix serverless and provisioned instances
  • Works with global databases and RDS Proxy
  • As of 5 November 2026: older material separates v1 and v2; check
Exam tip

Spiky or unknown load and you do not want to size instances: Aurora Serverless.

Read Replicas, Endpoints and Connections

  • RDS read replicas are asynchronous copies you create yourself; RDS does not autoscale them
  • Aurora Replicas share storage; Aurora Auto Scaling can add or remove them
  • Send reads to the reader endpoint or replica endpoints; the application must split reads and writes
  • Cross-Region replicas serve local reads and disaster recovery
  • Replica data can lag: do not use it where reads must be current
  • RDS Proxy pools connections, useful for Lambda and spikes
Exam tip

Reads are the bottleneck: replicas. Connections are the bottleneck: RDS Proxy.

Amazon DynamoDB [Verify live]

Topic What to know
On-demand mode The default and recommended mode for most workloads; pay per request, no capacity planning
Provisioned mode You set reads and writes per second; best for steady, predictable load
Reads Eventually consistent by default; strongly consistent costs twice as much and is not available on global secondary indexes
Design A well-spread partition key avoids hot partitions
Global tables Multi-Region, multi-active replicas
  • As of 5 November 2026: global tables now offer strong consistency across Regions as an option
Exam tip

Unknown traffic: on-demand. Steady, forecastable traffic: provisioned.

Caching with ElastiCache, DAX and MemoryDB

Service What it is Use it for
Amazon ElastiCache In-memory store for Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached; serverless or node-based A cache in front of any database, sessions, leaderboards
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) A DynamoDB-compatible cache; microsecond reads of eventually consistent data Read-heavy DynamoDB with hot keys; not for write-heavy or strongly consistent reads
Amazon MemoryDB A durable in-memory database: Multi-AZ transaction log A primary database that needs microsecond speed
Exam tip

A cache in front of a database: ElastiCache or DAX. A durable in-memory primary: MemoryDB.

Purpose-Built Databases

Service Model Highlights
Amazon DocumentDB Document, MongoDB-compatible Storage grows automatically; up to 15 replicas; data in three AZs
Amazon Neptune Graph: Gremlin, openCypher, SPARQL Recommendations, fraud detection, knowledge graphs; up to 15 replicas
Amazon Keyspaces Wide-column, Cassandra-compatible Serverless; run existing Cassandra code
Amazon Redshift Data warehouse Analytics on large data (module 13)
Exam tip

Match the data model: documents, graph, Cassandra or warehouse.

3Migration, the database chooser and practice

Migrating Databases

Migration Example Approach
Homogeneous MySQL to RDS or Aurora MySQL Snapshots, native tools, replication, or DMS
Heterogeneous Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL Convert the schema with DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT, then DMS moves the data
  • AWS DMS runs one-time migrations or ongoing replication, so the source can stay online until cutover
  • DMS Fleet Advisor inventories databases to plan
  • Data is encrypted at rest and in flight
Exam tip

Same engine: native tools. Different engine: convert the schema, then DMS.

Choosing a Database

  • Relational with transactions: RDS or Aurora
  • Key-value at massive scale: DynamoDB
  • Microsecond reads: ElastiCache, DAX or MemoryDB
  • Relationships: Neptune
  • MongoDB or Cassandra code: DocumentDB or Keyspaces

Exam tip

The access pattern, not the brand, picks the database.

What the Exam Asks: High-Performing Databases

  • Which database type for the data and access pattern
  • Which engine or compatibility: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle or SQL Server
  • Which capacity approach: Provisioned IOPS, on-demand, provisioned or serverless
  • Which replica or cache removes the bottleneck
  • Which migration path: homogeneous or heterogeneous
Exam tip

Underline read-heavy, write-heavy, spiky, relational or connected.

Design Check: Lantern and Loom Chooses Databases

Requirement Design
Orders with transactions and SQL Aurora (MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible)
Browsing overloads the primary Aurora Replicas behind the reader endpoint, plus a cache
Carts need millisecond lookups DynamoDB on-demand
A few hot product keys DAX in front of DynamoDB
Spiky weekend load on a new database Aurora Serverless
Recommendations from relationships Amazon Neptune
Move the self-managed MySQL Aurora MySQL by snapshot or replication
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Lantern and Loom's order system needs a managed relational database compatible with MySQL, with fast failover, storage that grows automatically and many read replicas. Which service fits best?

  • AAmazon DynamoDB with global tables
  • BAmazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition
  • CAmazon Neptune, a managed graph database
  • DAmazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache
Show the answer

Answer: B. Aurora is a MySQL-compatible relational engine whose storage grows automatically, with up to 15 replicas and fast failover. DynamoDB is key-value, Neptune is a graph database, and ElastiCache is an in-memory cache.

S2The shopping-cart service of Lantern and Loom needs single-digit millisecond lookups by cart ID, traffic that is unpredictable, and no capacity planning. Which design fits?

  • AA DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode
  • BA single large RDS instance with Provisioned IOPS
  • CA Redshift cluster
  • DAn S3 bucket with one object per cart
Show the answer

Answer: A. DynamoDB on-demand mode scales automatically for unpredictable traffic with no capacity planning, and serves key lookups in single-digit milliseconds. The other options are not built for high-rate key lookups.

S3A small set of popular products at Lantern and Loom is read thousands of times a second from a DynamoDB table, and slightly stale data is acceptable. The team wants microsecond reads with minimal code change. What should the architect add?

  • AA strongly consistent read setting on every request
  • BA larger provisioned write capacity
  • CAn Aurora replica
  • DA DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster
Show the answer

Answer: D. DAX is a DynamoDB-compatible in-memory cache that serves eventually consistent reads in microseconds with minimal code changes. Strongly consistent reads bypass the cache benefit, write capacity does not speed reads, and Aurora is a different database.

S4A new reporting database at Lantern and Loom will have an unknown, spiky load for its first months, and the team does not want to choose an instance size. Which option fits best?

  • AThe largest RDS instance class, sized for the worst case
  • BA Multi-AZ standby instance sized for the peak load
  • CAurora Serverless with a minimum and a maximum capacity
  • DA self-managed database on an EC2 instance
Show the answer

Answer: C. Aurora Serverless adjusts capacity in small steps between the limits you set, so you pay for what the workload uses and need not guess an instance size. A fixed large instance wastes money, a standby does not add capacity, and self-managing adds work.

S5Which TWO statements about Amazon DynamoDB are correct? (Select TWO.)

  • AOn-demand mode is the default and recommended option for most workloads
  • BEventually consistent reads cost twice as much as strongly consistent reads
  • CStrongly consistent reads are not supported on global secondary indexes
  • DProvisioned mode charges only for the capacity that was actually consumed
  • EDAX is the best choice for write-intensive tables
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. On-demand mode is the recommended default, and reads from global secondary indexes are always eventually consistent. Eventually consistent reads cost half as much, provisioned mode charges for the capacity provisioned, and DAX suits read-heavy tables.

S6Lantern and Loom must move an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime. Which approach fits?

  • ARestore an Oracle backup file directly into the Aurora PostgreSQL cluster
  • BConvert the schema, then migrate with AWS DMS and ongoing replication
  • CRestore a snapshot of an RDS MySQL instance into the Aurora cluster
  • DCopy the Oracle data files to S3 and attach them to the Aurora cluster
Show the answer

Answer: B. Moving between different engines is a heterogeneous migration: convert the schema and code first, then use DMS to load the data and replicate changes until cutover. A backup or snapshot from another engine cannot be restored into Aurora PostgreSQL.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Types relational, key-value, in-memory, document, graph, wide-column
Relational RDS by default, Aurora for scale and fast failover, Serverless for spiky load
DynamoDB on-demand for unknown, provisioned for steady; DAX for hot reads
Scale reads replicas, reader endpoint, caches, RDS Proxy
Migrate native tools if the engine is the same; schema conversion plus DMS if not
